newsitem.title: USA: EMU delay possible but unlikely - German official.
newsitem.headline: EMU delay possible but unlikely - German official.

text.p: A senior German Finance Ministry official said he could not exclude the possibility that the launch of European monetary union might be delayed, but added he did not think that was likely.

"For me, the most likely outcome is that we will start on time," Klaus Regling, Director General for European and International Financial Relations at the ministry, said. "But we can't exclude the other possibility."
Regling told a conference sponsored by the International Monetary Fund that the picture should become clearer during the course of this year.
He made his comments on Tuesday, but they could not be published until Wednesday under an agreement between the press and the IMF.

Financial markets have been abuzz with rumors that the Jan. 1, 1999 start of EMU will be delayed because of the difficulties that many countries, particularly Germany, face in meeting the Maastricht budget criteria for this year.
Under the Treaty, nations that wish to join the union must try to reduce their budget deficits this year to the equivalent of three percent of gross domestic product (GDP).
"Germany will insist on a strict and narrow interpretation of the convergence criteria (in Maastricht)," Regling said.
Regling voiced confidence that Germany would achieve its forecast of 2.4 percent economic growth this year and a reduction in the budget deficit to 2.9 pct of GDP.

"As of today, the German government sees no need to change that forecast," he said. But, he added, "If later in the year the data looks differently, the government would be prepared to adopt additional measures."
Regling said that Germany would not resort to what he called "creative accounting" or one-off measures to achieve the deficit target this year, as some other European nations have done.
That means that underlying budget deficits of those countries might be 3-1/2 or even four percent of GDP this year, even though the actual outturn would be lower, he said.
"Additional flexibility (in interpreting the Maastricht Treaty criteria for budget deficits) would not be warranted (in those cases)," he said.
Regling admitted though that Germany would not be able to meet the Maastricht target for a reduction in government debt to or toward the equivalent of 60 percent of GDP.
Debt stood at 60.3 percent of gdp at the end of last year and will probably increase a bit further this year, he said. "There's not much we can do about that," he added.

Regling argued that the debt target in the Treaty did not carry the same weight as the deficit target and partly blamed Germany's bloated public debt on the costs of paying for unification after the fall of the Communist bloc.
Even after 1997, European countries that join EMU must press ahead with cuts in their budget deficits, he said.
"These deficits have to be significantly reduced further over the next two to three years, as a minimum by, let's say, a half percent of gdp per year," Regling said.
The German official said that European nations must also press ahead with efforts to restructure their economies and make them more flexible, including the labor market.
Rather than solving structural problems, "EMU could very well make structural problems worse" if countries do not act, he said.
